subject: zoology
question_text: List out the extant orders of the Class Reptilia. Give two examples for each order.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.39, SAQ 34). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. ANSWERABILITY: the question asks for two examples per order, but Rhynchocephalia has only one living genus (Sphenodon), so a second example does not exist. The card says so rather than inventing one. BOOK WORDING: the book prints 'Najanaja' and 'chained viper'; the accepted forms are Naja naja and chain viper (Russell's viper), and the card uses those.

steps.label: Chelonia
steps.margin_note: Say what extant means in the first line, then take the four orders in order.
lines: Extant means the orders that are still living.
There are four living orders of Reptilia.
The body is covered by a hard shell of bony
plates. Teeth are absent; the jaws carry a
steps.why: The word extant is the first thing to settle, because the class also holds large extinct orders and a list that includes them is the commonest way to lose this whole question.
common_mistakes: Listing dinosaurs or pterosaurs. Extant means still living, so extinct orders do not belong.
Giving three orders. There are FOUR living orders.
steps.memory_tip: Four living orders: shell, beak head, crocodile, scale. One word each.

steps.label: Rhynchocephalia
steps.margin_note: One example only, with the reason. An honest line here reads better than a made up name.
lines: This order has only ONE living genus, so it is
Because only one genus survives, a second
example cannot be given for this order.
steps.why: This order is remembered by the fact that almost nothing is left of it, so the single surviving name is easier to hold than a list.
common_mistakes: Inventing a second example to match the question. Only Sphenodon survives; say so instead.
Writing that Sphenodon lives in Australia. It is restricted to New Zealand.
steps.memory_tip: One order, one genus, one country: Sphenodon in New Zealand.

steps.label: Crocodilia
steps.margin_note: Two examples are asked; three are printed. Two named genera earn the mark.
lines: They are large aquatic reptiles. The heart is
completely four chambered, which no other
steps.why: The four chambered heart is the character that makes Crocodilia stand out from every other reptile, so it is worth one line even in a list question.
common_mistakes: Writing that crocodiles have a three chambered heart. Their heart is completely four chambered.
Putting the gharial in a separate order. Gavialis belongs to Crocodilia.
steps.memory_tip: The only reptile with a full four chambered heart is the crocodile.

steps.label: Squamata
steps.margin_note: Split the order into lizards and snakes, then name examples. This step carries the most names.
lines: This is the largest order. It has two groups.
steps.why: Squamata is split into lizards and snakes before the examples are given, because the examiner expects both groups to appear under the one order.
common_mistakes: Listing snakes as a separate order. Snakes and lizards are two groups INSIDE Squamata.
Giving only lizards. Both groups must be shown for the full mark.
steps.memory_tip: Squama means scale, so every scaly reptile — lizard and snake alike — sits here.

insider_note: Four orders, one mark each, and the mark is for the ORDER NAME plus its examples — a beautiful description of turtles with the word Chelonia missing scores nothing.
